objectives: Given the facts of one volunteer role, write a role description that says what, when, where, why, which checks are needed and who to contact, with every fact checked and your contact information added

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing a clear volunteer role description
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a role description that tells a volunteer exactly what, when, where and why.
This lesson builds toward: Given the facts of one volunteer role, you will write a role description that says what, when, where, why, which checks are needed and who to contact, with every fact checked and your contact information added.
People say yes when they know exactly what they are signing up for. A vague ask like "We need help!" gets few replies. A clear role gets more.
A good role description answers: What will I do? When and for how long? Where? What skills or checks are needed (for example, a background check to work with children)? Why does it matter? Who do I contact?
Give AI the facts and ask it to write them up. For example: "Write a short volunteer role description for a Saturday food pantry helper, 9 am to noon twice a month, lifting up to 20 pounds, no experience needed. Warm and clear, under 150 words."
Step by step:
- Write down the tasks, schedule, place and any requirements.
- Write one sentence on why the role matters.
- Ask AI to turn your notes into a short role description.
- Check every fact and add your contact information yourself.
Words to know:
- Role description: a short write-up of a volunteer job: tasks, time, place, needs and purpose.
- Background check: a check of someone's records, often required to work with children or vulnerable people.
Try it now: Pick one real volunteer role your organization needs. Write the facts, ask AI for a role description under 150 words, and correct anything that is wrong.
You can now write a clear volunteer role description with AI's help.

check.q: Why does a clear role description get more replies?
options: People say yes when they know exactly what they are signing up for
check.why: A vague ask gets few replies; a clear role gets more.

check.q: Your tutoring role works with children. What must the description mention?
options: That a background check is needed
check.why: A role description says which checks are needed, such as a background check to work with children.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Drafting recruitment posts and emails
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn one role description into a social media post and a supporter email.
This lesson builds toward: Given your role description, you will write a short social media post and a supporter email with AI, each with one call to action and only made-up or approved stories.
Different places need different lengths. A social media post is short and friendly with one clear action. An email to supporters can tell a little story and give more detail.
Ask AI for both from the same role description: "Using this role description, write a 50-word Facebook post with one call to action, and a 150-word email to our supporters that starts with a short story about a family we serve." Use a made-up or approved story, never a real person's private details without permission.
Ask for a few versions and pick the one that sounds most like you. Add the real sign-up link yourself.
Step by step:
- Paste your role description into the AI.
- Ask for a short social post with one call to action.
- Ask for a longer supporter email.
- Ask for two versions of each and pick one.
- Add your real sign-up link and check the details.
Words to know:
- Call to action: the one thing you ask the reader to do, like "Sign up here".
- Supporters: people who already know and care about your organization: donors, members, past volunteers.
Try it now: Use your role description from Lesson 1 to get a 50-word social post and a 150-word supporter email. Pick the best version of each and edit it.
You can now create recruitment posts and emails for different audiences from one role description.

check.q: Which is longer and can tell a little story?
check.why: A social post is short; a supporter email can tell a story and give more detail.

check.q: AI's post has no sign-up link. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to invent a link
Add the real sign-up link yourself
check.why: Add the real sign-up link yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reaching new kinds of volunteers
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to brainstorm where to find volunteers and how to make roles easier to join.
This lesson builds toward: For your community, you will list new places to find volunteers and ways to make the role easier to join, with every group or site checked as real before contacting it.
Many organizations ask the same few people again and again. AI is good at brainstorming new places to look: local colleges and high schools that need service hours, employers with volunteer days, faith communities, senior centers, and online volunteer listing sites.
Ask AI: "List 10 places in a mid-sized city to recruit weekend food pantry volunteers, and one sentence to say to each." Check that any group or site it names is real before you contact it.
Also ask how to make roles easier to say yes to: shorter shifts, family-friendly roles, remote tasks such as making calls or writing cards, and materials in the languages your community speaks.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a list of places to find volunteers.
- Ask for one sentence to say to each.
- Check that each place or site is real.
- Ask how to make the role easier to join.
- Pick your top three places to try.
Words to know:
- Service hours: volunteer hours that schools or programs ask students to complete.
- Remote task: volunteer work done from home, such as calls, cards or online help.
Try it now: Ask AI for 10 places to recruit volunteers for your role in your area. Check them, then choose your top three and write down who you will contact.
You can now find new sources of volunteers and make roles easier to join.

check.q: Which is a remote task that makes a role easier to join?
check.why: Remote tasks such as making calls or writing cards are easier to say yes to.

check.q: Many families you serve speak Spanish, and you want them to volunteer too. What helps?
options: Offer materials in the languages your community speaks
check.why: Materials in your community's languages make roles easier to join.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Signing up, welcoming and keeping volunteers

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a simple sign-up form
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a short online sign-up form and ask only what you need.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Forms or Microsoft Forms, you will create a short sign-up form that asks only what you need, with no sensitive details asked and the form tested by you.
A free form tool such as Google Forms or Microsoft Forms lets people sign up from a link. Answers go into a spreadsheet you control.
Ask only what you need: name, email or phone, which shifts they can do, and anything you must know (such as language skills). Do not ask for Social Security numbers, birth dates or other sensitive details on a simple form. If a background check is needed, use your organization's approved process.
AI can suggest questions and wording: "Suggest 6 short sign-up form questions for a food pantry volunteer role." You build the form yourself, and the answers stay in your form tool, not in the AI.
Step by step:
- Open Google Forms or Microsoft Forms and start a blank form.
- Ask AI to suggest short questions.
- Keep only what you truly need.
- Add the shift choices as checkboxes.
- Test the form yourself, then copy the share link.
Words to know:
- Form: an online set of questions people fill in; answers are saved for you.
- Sensitive details: information that could harm someone if shared, like ID numbers or health details.
Try it now: Build a sign-up form for your role with no more than six questions. Fill it in yourself to test it, and copy the link into your recruitment post.
You can now build a short, safe volunteer sign-up form.

check.q: Where do sign-up answers go in a free form tool?
check.why: Answers go into a spreadsheet you control.

check.q: The role needs a background check. How do you handle it?
options: Add Social Security number to the simple form
Ask for birth dates on the form
Use your organization's approved background check process
check.why: Do not collect sensitive details on a simple form; use the approved process.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Welcome and reminder messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write a welcome message and a reminder that make new volunteers feel ready.
This lesson builds toward: For a new volunteer, you will write a welcome message and a reminder with placeholders, with date, time, place, what to bring and a contact person.
The first few days decide whether a new volunteer comes back. A quick welcome makes people feel wanted and ready.
A good welcome says thank you, confirms the date, time and place, says what to wear or bring, names a contact person, and says what the first shift will be like. A reminder a few days before repeats the key details.
Ask AI for both, using placeholders: "Write a warm welcome email for a new food pantry volunteer. Use [name], [shift date], [contact person]. Under 120 words." Then fill in details using your email tool or mail merge, not the AI.
Step by step:
- List what a new volunteer needs to know.
- Ask AI for a welcome message with placeholders.
- Ask AI for a short reminder for a few days before.
- Fill in details in your email tool.
- Check every date and time.
Words to know:
- Onboarding: helping a new volunteer get ready: welcome, training and first shift.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like [name] that you replace with the real detail later.
Try it now: Ask AI for a welcome email and a reminder text with placeholders for your role. Edit both so they sound like your organization.
You can now write welcome and reminder messages that help new volunteers show up ready.

check.q: What decides whether a new volunteer comes back?
check.why: The first few days decide whether a new volunteer comes back.

check.q: A new volunteer starts Saturday and has not heard from you. What do you send first?
options: A warm welcome with date, time, place, what to bring and a contact
check.why: A good welcome confirms the details and names a contact so they feel ready.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Thanking and keeping volunteers
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple plan to thank volunteers and learn why they stay or leave.
This lesson builds toward: For the volunteers you recruit, you will plan how you will thank them, share results and ask for feedback, with dates on your calendar.
Keeping a volunteer is easier than finding a new one. People stay when they feel thanked, useful and part of a team.
Simple ways to thank: a personal note after the first shift, sharing what their work made possible ("Saturday's team packed 300 boxes"), recognition at a gathering, and asking their ideas. AI can help write thank-you notes and short surveys, such as three questions about what went well and what to change.
Write a short plan: when you will thank people, how you will share results, and when you will ask for feedback. Then put it on your calendar.
Step by step:
- Plan a thank-you after the first shift.
- Plan how you will share results with volunteers.
- Ask AI to draft a three-question feedback survey.
- Put the thank-you and survey dates on your calendar.
Words to know:
- Retention: keeping volunteers coming back over time.
- Feedback survey: a few questions that ask people what went well and what to change.
Try it now: Final task: put your full recruitment kit together: role description, social post, email, sign-up form, welcome message, reminder and thank-you plan. Edit each piece and check every detail.
You can now recruit, welcome and keep volunteers with AI-drafted messages you have checked and made your own.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Role description Missing what, when, where, why or who to contact. Answers what, when, where, why, any checks needed and who to contact. Short, warm and checked by someone who knows the role. Post and email No clear call to action, or a real person's story used without permission. A short post and a supporter email, each with one action and the real sign-up link. Learner tried versions and chose the one that sounds most like the organization. Sign-up form Asks for sensitive details or was not tested. A few simple questions asking only what is needed, tested by the learner. Asks about languages or shift choices that help match volunteers. Welcome and reminder Missing date, time, place or a contact person. Welcome and one-week reminder with all key details, using placeholders. Says what the first shift will be like and what to wear or bring. Thank-you plan No plan, or no dates. Says when to thank people, how to share results and when to ask for feedback, with dates. Includes a short feedback survey on what went well and what to change. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a simple way to thank volunteers?
options: Asking them to recruit five friends
Sharing what their work made possible
Giving them more shifts without asking
check.why: Sharing results, like boxes packed, shows volunteers their work matters.

check.q: You wrote a thank-you plan but keep forgetting it. What do you do?
options: Thank people only once a year
Put each step on your calendar with dates
check.why: Write the plan and put it on your calendar.
